The monsoon had turned the lane outside Chetan's rented room in Andheri into a brown stream, and for three weeks he had been waking at noon and studying past two. On the first Monday of July he taped a sheet above his desk: lights off by midnight, up at seven, two study blocks before lunch. Each night he wrote a tick or a cross. The first week had four crosses. The second had two. By the fourth week the sheet was nearly all ticks, and his accounts mock score had climbed from forty-one to sixty-three.
Sabina, from his tutorial group, leaned over the sheet while dripping rain onto his floor. "You made this yourself?"
"Yeah." Chetan tapped the column of ticks. "Turns out the mornings were mine to take back." He sounded a little surprised at his own voice.

qa.q: What did Chetan tape above his desk on the first Monday of July?
qa.a: He taped a sheet with his plan: lights off by midnight, up at seven, and two study blocks before lunch.

qa.q: What does Chetan's surprised tone suggest he is feeling when he shows Sabina the sheet?
qa.a: He feels proud and newly confident, because the ticks and the jump from forty-one to sixty-three show him that his own choices changed the result.

qa.q: What would help Chetan keep this going after exams?
qa.a: He could keep a smaller version of the tick sheet and review it every Sunday, so he notices early if late nights creep back.

qa.q: How might Sabina see Chetan differently after reading the sheet?
qa.a: Sabina may see Chetan as someone who can steer his own routine, and it might make Sabina wonder whether a simple record could help with study too.

grounding: A student sets and tracks a new sleep and study routine, and the visible results show him that he shaped the outcome.

subtype: Everything is luck or teacher's mood [Actor]
passage:
Monday, before Pongal. Sarika got her maths test back: eleven out of twenty. "Miss was in a bad mood," she told Lalit at the water tap. "She cut marks for everything." Lalit had also got eleven. He shrugged and said he hadn't finished the practice sheet.
Wednesday, holidays nearly here. Sarika's revision book stayed in her bag. "No point," she said, drawing kolam patterns in the margin. "It depends on Miss anyway."
Friday, after the holidays. The new test came back with nine. Lalit had fourteen. "You got lucky," Sarika said. Lalit said he did the practice sheet twice. Sarika was already looking at the window, sure that Monday's mood would decide the next one too.

qa.q: What mark did Sarika get on the test after the holidays?
qa.a: The new test came back with nine.

qa.q: Why does Sarika feel it is pointless to open her revision book?
qa.a: She is resigned and a bit defeated, because she believes the marks depend on Miss's mood, so studying feels like it would change nothing.

qa.q: What could a teacher or parent try to help Sarika?
qa.a: They could sit with her and match the questions she got wrong to the practice sheet, so she can see how preparing changes the marks.

qa.q: How might Lalit see the difference between his score and Sarika's?
qa.a: He probably links his fourteen to doing the practice sheet twice, so Sarika calling it luck may confuse or annoy him.

grounding: A child blames the teacher's mood for low marks, never connects results with preparation, and her effort drops over the holidays.

passage:
Saturday, three days before Christmas. Jaya heard her parents arguing about the electricity bill while the plastic tree blinked in the corner. She went to her room and thought: if I hadn't asked for the new school shoes, there'd be money. She lay awake counting everything she had asked for that year.
Tuesday. Zubin texted that he'd skipped tuition again to hang out at the station. Jaya stared at the message. I should've made him come with me. I should've said something last week. She apologised to him twice, though he hadn't asked.
Christmas Day. Her mother hugged her at breakfast and said the bill was sorted. Jaya smiled, but inside she was already listing what she'd done wrong this time, as if every quarrel and every choice in her world had passed through her hands first.

qa.q: What were Jaya's parents arguing about?
qa.a: They were arguing about the electricity bill.

qa.q: What is Jaya feeling when she apologises to Zubin twice?
qa.a: She feels guilty and anxious, because she believes she should have stopped him skipping tuition, as if his choices were hers to control.

qa.q: What could help Jaya when she starts listing her mistakes?
qa.a: She could write down who actually made each choice, such as her parents and Zubin, and talk the list through with a trusted adult like her mother or a school counsellor.

qa.q: If you were Zubin, how might you feel receiving Jaya's apologies?
qa.a: Zubin might feel puzzled or even uncomfortable, since he made the choice to skip tuition himself and never asked her to say sorry.

grounding: A teenager blames herself for her parents' argument and a friend's choices, showing how too much felt control becomes guilt.

passage:
The office emptied early during the last week of Ramzan, and Zeenat stayed back to watch the sales board refresh. Her target bar sat at half again.
"Third quarter running," Darshan said, pulling a chair over. "What happened with the hospital account?"
"The boss gave them to me late. And the market's dead. Some people just get the easy clients." She scrolled past the call log without opening it.
Darshan hesitated. "I noticed the follow-up mails went out a week after the demos. Maybe that's worth a look?"
"Everyone sends late mails. That's not it." Zeenat closed the laptop harder than she meant to. "When my luck turns, the numbers will too."
Darshan nodded and left the log on the shared drive anyway. She did not open it before the iftar call sounded from the street.

qa.q: Where did Darshan leave the call log?
qa.a: Darshan left the log on the shared drive.

qa.q: Why might Zeenat refuse to look at the late follow-up mails?
qa.a: Looking would sting her pride, so blaming the boss and the market feels safer and protects her from feeling ashamed about her own part.

qa.q: What small step could help Zeenat break the pattern?
qa.a: She could open the call log once and mark which delays were hers, perhaps with Darshan, and change one habit such as sending follow-ups the same day.

qa.q: What is it like for Darshan when Zeenat brushes off the point about late mails?
qa.a: Darshan probably feels awkward and a bit shut out, having raised it gently and still got a hard close of the laptop, yet cared enough to leave the log.

grounding: An adult blames her boss, the market and luck for repeated shortfalls and will not examine her own delays, which guards her pride but blocks learning.

passage:
Summer puzzle club, week three. Note for Preeti's family.
Preeti arrived today holding her uncle Vishal's hand; he told me again, "She's our little genius, she never gets anything wrong." Preeti smiled but went quiet.
When I put out the harder grid puzzles, Preeti chose the easy ones she had finished last week. I asked her to try a new grid. She said, "I don't want to," and when a square wouldn't fit she pushed the sheet away and scowled. Later she told me softly, "If I get it wrong, I won't be clever anymore."
Next I sat beside her and we solved one row together. I praised how she tested three numbers before one fitted. She tried a second row alone.
Suggestion: at home, notice her trying, not her being smart.

qa.q: Which puzzles did Preeti choose when the harder grids came out?
qa.a: She chose the easy ones she had finished last week.

qa.q: Why does Preeti push the sheet away and scowl?
qa.a: She feels scared and angry, because a wrong answer seems to threaten the clever label she keeps hearing, and she worries she won't be clever anymore.

qa.q: How could Preeti's family support her at home?
qa.a: They could praise the way she tries, like testing different numbers, instead of calling her a genius who never gets things wrong.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Preeti's choice of easy puzzles if he only hears about her scores?
qa.a: Vishal might think she is simply doing well, without noticing that the genius label is making her avoid anything hard.

grounding: A child repeatedly called clever starts avoiding harder puzzles to protect that label, as seen by the adult running the club.

passage:
The power went out halfway through the monsoon fractions class, and rain drummed so loudly on the tin roof that Manjula Ma'am had to walk desk to desk instead of teaching from the board.
Tarun was stuck on the pizza problem. First he drew circles, but they came out uneven. Then he tried folding a strip of paper. That didn't work either. Finally he lined up twelve chalk marks and circled groups of three and four.
Manjula Ma'am crouched by his desk with her phone torch. "You tried circles, then paper, then lines. When one way failed, you switched. That's why you got it."
Tarun looked at his messy page. "So being stuck is part of it?"
"It is. Want to try the tougher one on page forty?"
He nodded and turned the page before the lights came back.

qa.q: What did Tarun line up to finally solve the pizza problem?
qa.a: He lined up twelve chalk marks and circled groups of three and four.

qa.q: What does Tarun's question "So being stuck is part of it?" suggest he is thinking?
qa.a: He is starting to feel encouraged and curious, seeing that switching methods, not being naturally good, is what made it work.

qa.q: Which choice by Manjula Ma'am worked, and why?
qa.a: She named each method Tarun tried and linked switching to success, which made him willing to take on the tougher problem.

qa.q: What might change if Manjula Ma'am had only said "You're so good at maths"?
qa.a: Tarun might have felt proud for a moment but less keen to risk the harder page, since there would be nothing to repeat except being good.

grounding: A teacher praises a child's switching of methods during a power cut, and the child chooses a harder problem next.

The art portfolio was due the Monday after Holi, and Yash had three days left, most of them booked for his cousin's wedding. Friday evening he sat on the balcony with a pencil, trying to draw the neem tree. The trunk came out like a pipe. He erased it twice and tore the paper.
Gopika, his sister, still had pink colour on her ears from the morning. "Want me to show you the shading trick?"
"No point. Some people are just born artists. I'm not creative. I'll take the zero." He put the pencil back in the box and snapped it shut.
"You've drawn for, what, twenty minutes this year?"
"That's what I'm saying. It's not in me." He went inside and switched on the cricket. The blank page stayed on the balcony chair, curling in the heat.

qa.q: What was Yash trying to draw on the balcony?
qa.a: He was trying to draw the neem tree.

qa.q: Why does giving up feel reasonable to Yash?
qa.a: He feels frustrated and a little embarrassed, and telling himself he is just not creative makes quitting feel like accepting a fact instead of failing.

qa.q: What would you advise Yash with the deadline so close?
qa.a: He could accept Gopika's shading trick and aim to finish one small, rough drawing, treating it as practice rather than proof of talent.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel when Yash turns down her help?
qa.a: Gopika may feel brushed off and a bit sad, since she can see he has hardly practised and is giving up far too early.

grounding: A teenager who draws poorly decides he is simply not creative and stops, turning his current level into a fixed limit.

passage:
Last Onam, the design studio pinned the semester projects in the corridor, and I walked past mine to stand in front of Irfan's. He had built a bamboo shelter model that folded flat. Our professor had written, "Studio should see this."
Mine was a neat, safe bus stop. Everyone said "nice" and moved on.
I told myself Irfan was just born with it. His father is an architect; he probably sketched before he could talk. I remember the tight feeling in my chest when my own friends crowded round his model. It felt like every compliment he got was taken from me.
When my roommate called out, "Karthik, come see how he did the joints," I said I had a class and left. I didn't have a class. I just couldn't look at it any longer.

qa.q: What had the professor written on Irfan's project?
qa.a: The professor had written, "Studio should see this."

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when friends crowded round Irfan's model?
qa.a: Karthik felt envious and threatened, a tight feeling in the chest, because every compliment to Irfan seemed like something taken away.

qa.q: What could Karthik try instead of walking away next time?
qa.a: Karthik could go and look at how Irfan did the joints and ask him a question, treating the model as something to learn from.

qa.q: What would change if Karthik saw Irfan's skill as learned rather than inborn?
qa.a: The gap might feel like a path to follow instead of a fixed verdict, and Irfan's success might inspire rather than hurt.

grounding: A student decides a gifted peer's lead is destiny and feels threatened by the praise instead of inspired.
